$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{3}{y}\,i-\frac{2}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-5)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-5(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-10\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186369291 :question/id #uuid "15f53228-e106-54bd-8baa-01a5e8c54996" :question/math-academy-id "q-125484" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179741 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "976e05d4-59a8-5a93-be2f-b22357f388b9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Circulation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2433c883-9454-5783-a42b-a158449a6704" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-6\pi " :db/id 17592186369293} {:answer/id #uuid "da8f4541-beae-50fa-837a-88c5c1315ce2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2\pi " :db/id 17592186369294} {:answer/id #uuid "94ddba9c-b5d2-5aad-bbd2-1982a2662332" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6\pi " :db/id 17592186369295} {:answer/id #uuid "759a9631-bed4-55f7-ba67-742c0198c7c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186369296} {:answer/id #uuid "40433ff5-a4f9-59d7-b1cf-0b7ff6dd7d8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186369297}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "40433ff5-a4f9-59d7-b1cf-0b7ff6dd7d8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186369297} :answer-field/id #uuid "e70cc117-b909-56f1-8961-8a545df9549f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186369292}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=2x\,i+2y\,j$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8(\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-4(-1+1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415313 :question/id #uuid "4ec2acb3-1493-5600-bce3-9a9694ba6ec0" :question/math-academy-id "q-125470"} {:db/id 17592186415315 :question/id #uuid "b79e3fb3-3865-5932-ba2e-8b5992286bc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-125481"} {:db/id 17592186455447 :question/id #uuid "442b3fed-648b-5cc8-977b-6700ae26738b" :question/math-academy-id "q-125482" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7d45a6-b7b5-5b6e-a82c-a1748d83e603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9\pi " :db/id 17592186454946} {:answer/id #uuid "7e4f36c3-2d0c-50c9-a36d-272fd914e84a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186455133} {:answer/id #uuid "c26f1bdf-26e0-5acd-bbc9-1a8e6be78f5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\pi " :db/id 17592186455239} {:answer/id #uuid "c3275529-012a-5a31-82a4-2f28fcd1acb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186455240} {:answer/id #uuid "ff6f64d6-184a-5394-8a28-a8c004572db7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\pi " :db/id 17592186455340}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455240} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbf611c1-7a64-56ff-a8ce-599f171848cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186179743 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179605 :question/id #uuid "1e15ae93-0a63-506a-a0ae-b15e035f0494" :question/math-academy-id "e-9543"} :knowledge-point/id :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =( e^y+x)\,\mathbf i +(xe^y+y^2)\,\mathbf j.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $\mathbf F$ is conservative

- $\displaystyle\int\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = 0$ for any piecewise-smooth path $C\in\mathbb R^2$

- $\displaystyle\oint\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r =0$ for any closed path $C\in\mathbb R^2$" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf F$ is a conservative vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ then the circulation $\Gamma = 0$ for any *closed* path $C\in\mathbb R^2,$ that is 

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = 0.
$$

We notice that $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field with domain $D = \mathbb R^2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} =  e^y.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. The vector field $\mathbf F$ is conservative since the partial derivatives are equal and continuous everywhere on $\mathbb R^2.$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. The result $\Gamma = 0$ applies to closed curves only.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186049150} {:db/id 17592186180026 :question/id #uuid "76c1a939-3dff-51ed-a845-c6333747802b" :question/math-academy-id "q-125424" 17592186180496 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180719 :tutorial/content "Given a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and a path $C$ defined by $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ the line integral 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r
$$

gives the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from the initial point $\mathbf{r}(a)$ to the terminal point $\mathbf{r}(b)$ on the curve.

Now suppose that $C$ is a *closed* curve. The **circulation** of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C,$ denoted using the Greek letter $\Gamma$ (pronounced "gamma"), is given by the line integral

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Remember that the notation $\displaystyle\oint$ simply reminds us that we're integrating along a closed path.

The circulation $\Gamma$ gives the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along the entire closed path. We can also think of $\Gamma$ as a measure of how much $\mathbf F$ circulates around $C.$

Let's build some intuition by considering some examples. 

- Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction, shown below. 

![](images/9e/9e9de4e3734be4f7d8f59f6d54d0ed92c51db3a0beb8277f4b450531b7dab332.png)

It's clear from the picture that $\mathbf{F}$ *assists* the motion of a particle as it moves counterclockwise along the path. Therefore, we can conclude that

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r >    0.
$$

- Now imagine that $C$ is traversed in the clockwise direction.

![](images/16/16dd701d51e3b43714b58993f66e42359289f557ef86fd9091ab6b8bba7041e7.png)

We see that $\mathbf F$ works *against* the particle's motion as it moves clockwise along the path. Therefore,

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

- Finally, consider the vector field $\mathbf{G}$ and the closed curve $C$ traversed in the clockwise direction, shown below.

![](images/8b/8bf269cecceeefc3e81b868a4fc4c54127f00432145782b24719bb49552868c7.png)

Since the force $\mathbf G$ acts perpendicular to the particle's motion as it moves around the path, it neither helps nor hinders its motion. Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf G\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4446c197-397c-5e41-a7a9-22d57126ffae" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5833 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2145b39b-47ee-5ae2-ad16-55a2719cc2e0" :step/math-academy-id 35732 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180494}} {:db/id 17592186180499 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179743 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179605 :question/id #uuid "1e15ae93-0a63-506a-a0ae-b15e035f0494" :question/math-academy-id "e-9543"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1da220a9-2afc-5b63-a423-a4d2b3de9567" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049150}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180026} {:db/id 17592186180027} {:db/id 17592186259836} {:db/id 17592186259837} {:db/id 17592186259838} {:db/id 17592186259839} {:db/id 17592186259840} {:db/id 17592186259842} {:db/id 17592186369298} {:db/id 17592186369305} {:db/id 17592186369312} {:db/id 17592186415314}] :knowledge-point/title "Circulation in Conservative Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "3bb98ffd-856f-5d48-bd6b-55f3885cdca8" :step/math-academy-id 35749} {:db/id 17592186180500 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180721 :tutorial/content "The fundamental theorem of line integrals states that

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a))
$$

 

where $C$ is a piecewise-smooth curve $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and $f$ is differentiable function such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ 

Now, if $C$ is a closed path that's traversed once, then $\mathbf r(a) = \mathbf r(b),$ and we have

$$
\Gamma = \oint_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = 0.
$$

Therefore, the circulation of a conservative vector field around *any* closed path equals zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "5bc343b6-5187-5353-bb7b-23db12eaa417" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5836 :tutorial/title "Circulation in Conservative Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "345a9b9c-ae65-5c52-85e2-8ffa7905b813" :step/math-academy-id 35756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180499}}] :activity/title "Circulation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179865} {:db/id 17592186180496 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180719 :tutorial/content "Given a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and a path $C$ defined by $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ the line integral

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the **clockwise** direction. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$

II. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$

III. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement III is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/c4/c498ddeae8ba4325a4a1dfc0840520c4718bb50a0600970405374dde933e1b1d.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement II is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.

![](images/74/740429a29b5eb4b72bbfae11e08c9ac272e72e31d395b4dad2602beb4d4ba40a.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} :step/id #uuid "23ee9455-766f-5586-95a2-a9ed8dfe87ce"} {:db/id 17592186455518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186455447 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7d45a6-b7b5-5b6e-a82c-a1748d83e603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9\pi " :db/id 17592186454946} {:answer/id #uuid "7e4f36c3-2d0c-50c9-a36d-272fd914e84a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186455133} {:answer/id #uuid "c26f1bdf-26e0-5acd-bbc9-1a8e6be78f5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\pi " :db/id 17592186455239} {:answer/id #uuid "c3275529-012a-5a31-82a4-2f28fcd1acb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186455240} {:answer/id #uuid "ff6f64d6-184a-5394-8a28-a8c004572db7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\pi " :db/id 17592186455340}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455240} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbf611c1-7a64-56ff-a8ce-599f171848cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "442b3fed-648b-5cc8-977b-6700ae26738b" :question/math-academy-id "q-125482" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "40211c38-7902-5a30-be18-54ba1e524e35" :step/next {:db/id 17592186455523}} {:db/id 17592186455515 :step/content {:db/id 17592186455499 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7781bfa2-360a-52f2-b8a7-5fd12172c6fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186455124} {:answer/id #uuid "7ad5e1c3-fe87-52c4-9343-a5e560de27a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186455128} {:answer/id #uuid "9a55b0b7-ffd1-54c4-8119-7e1a1a488949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186455185} {:answer/id #uuid "b6715a23-2351-5f62-8ba5-ef943e459d30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186455223} {:answer/id #uuid "c19b819d-c541-51b6-a6e0-7dae5f0106b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186455237}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455223} :answer-field/id #uuid "bd93af99-5bab-55c2-8a85-e0d5efec7517" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455405}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d78a254d-adb2-5551-a797-0a608524ca4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-125669" :question/problem "![](images/36/36ebce64036b7661c81aa6525c407f698375544532985175cc465ddc3ff4f5a8.png)

III. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$ 

![](images/85/8595904122fac3431fc959b2fa4aa5a3062bd1bffd1a391a0861fa12f2498054.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves **clockwise** along $C.$

![](images/f1/f1f31f2b6eefddedc46b8e845703904c0b4566963e64a644f7a4ab32bb7240c3.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

"62c34646-f7cf-5ffd-b957-4151bdbb5e44" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Left Riemann Sum in Sigma Notation"}] :question/problem "The area under the curve $y=4-x^2$ between $x=-1,$ $x=2,$ and the $x$-axis is approximated using a left Riemann sum, as shown below. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?

![](images/b5/b517da6e730ac50341b133a60ae8ab99cfed7b2ce92638e6028bb3fac6fbf9da.png)" :question/worked-solution "The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$ 

From the diagram, we see that there are $n=3$ rectangles. The endpoints indicate that $a=-1$ and $b=2,$ so the step size is

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{2-(-1)}{3} = \dfrac 3 3 = 1.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the left Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(a+kΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{3-1}f(-1+k\cdot 1)\cdot 1 \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}f(k-1) \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}(4-(k-1)^{2}) \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}(4-{k}^{2}+2k-1) \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{2}(3+2k-{k}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048363} {:db/id 17592186048922} {:db/id 17592186049317} {:db/id 17592186097266 :question/id #uuid "a4775a77-d771-53fd-b271-b9d95eb3c462" :question/math-academy-id "q-49185"} {:db/id 17592186097271 :question/id #uuid "7a82c733-fd67-5ad0-94b7-aa145f6ffd91" :question/math-academy-id "q-49264" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186096628 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "62c34646-f7cf-5ffd-b957-4151bdbb5e44" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Left Riemann Sum in Sigma Notation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b2858820-0886-5f21-935d-6d8d793f9364" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_(i = 0)^(2)\sqrt{i - 1}" :db/id 17592186095551} {:answer/id #uuid "d3ed1402-9ed7-5f03-a7a6-1b4955577c18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_(i = 1)^(3)\sqrt{i + 1}" :db/id 17592186095552} {:answer/id #uuid "0068062b-f325-5314-99d6-2d7fc8c369d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_(i = 0)^(2)\sqrt{i + 1}" :db/id 17592186095553} {:answer/id #uuid "28e394e2-ca7b-5b78-9d0e-664fd606743f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_(i = 0)^(2)\sqrt{i}" :db/id 17592186095554} {:answer/id #uuid "566cf112-3e87-5680-9076-4e2e5bb5025b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_(i = 0)^(2)\sqrt{i + 4}" :db/id 17592186095555}] :answer-field/id #uuid "c8832846-ab8f-51d9-b35e-38e81a04d8b6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186095550}] :question/problem "![](images/35/35b881e8bb04eb192967ebc94945850fb0450012675369facd4efb41c611aaab.png)

What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?" :question/worked-solution "The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\Delta x,
$$

where $x_i = a + i\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$ 

Note that here we are using the index $i$ instead of $k.$ It doesn't matter which letter we use for the counter.

We're told that there are $n=3$ subintervals. The endpoints indicate that $a=0$ and $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{3-0}{3} = \dfrac{3}{3} = 1.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(a+iΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}f(0+i\cdot 1)\cdot 1 \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}f(i) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{i}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049386} {:db/id 17592186097265 :question/id #uuid "b131859f-3e85-573d-bc1d-43ec042cf526" :question/math-academy-id "q-49184"} {:db/id 17592186097267 :question/id #uuid $$
{S}_{R}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx,

$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097443 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097908 :tutorial/content "Remember that the formula for the left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size over the interval $[a,b]$ is

$$
({\color{red}{f(x_0)}} + {\color{red}{f(x_1)}} + \ldots + {\color{red}{f(x_{n-1})}}) \cdot {\color{blue}{\Delta x}},
$$

where $n$ is the number of rectangles, $x_0=a$ and $x_{n}=b$ are the endpoints of the interval, and the step size is $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

The formula above contains a lot of addition signs. We can simplify this by writing the sum in the **sigma notation**:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} {\color{red}f(x_k)}\,{\color{blue}\Delta x},
$$

where $x_k = a+ k\Delta x$  for  $k=0,1,2,\ldots ,n-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "24aaf571-5125-51e2-baea-075b51bb9415" :tutorial/math-academy-id 751 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c6c39a44-fae6-59e4-a645-dca1c21bd8e7" :step/math-academy-id 1444 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097444}} {:db/id 17592186097444 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096628 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096428 :question/id #uuid "87747005-ce77-5ec6-9f44-af074633aa98" :question/math-academy-id "e-401"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "62c34646-f7cf-5ffd-b957-4151bdbb5e44" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048363} {:db/id 17592186048922} {:db/id 17592186049317}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097266} {:db/id 17592186097271} {:db/id 17592186233956} {:db/id 17592186233957} {:db/id 17592186233958} {:db/id 17592186234110} {:db/id 17592186234334} {:db/id 17592186234338} {:db/id 17592186234339} {:db/id 17592186297427} {:db/id 17592186297428} {:db/id 17592186317568}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Left Riemann Sum in Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "b882a5bd-1c56-5f3d-8a4f-5365c326314b" :step/math-academy-id 1445 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097445}} {:db/id 17592186097445 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097909 :tutorial/content "Recall that the formula for the right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[a,b]$ is

$$
({\color{red}f(x_1)} + {\color{red}f(x_2)}  + \ldots + {\color{red}f(x_n)}) \cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x}.
$$

This right Riemann sum in sigma notation is

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} {\color{red}f(x_k)}{\color{blue}\Delta x},
$$

where $x_k=a+k\Delta x$  and $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

Notice that this is very similar to the left Riemann sum. {:db/id 17592186049975} {:activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186163040} :activity/id #uuid "d215dc31-fcec-5081-8994-43caf3b19295" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050911 :topic/id #uuid "70a63868-505f-50a9-bb34-96c96024a1cb" :topic/math-academy-id 3138} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163310 :tutorial/content "The table below describes the number of classes taken per semester and the average final grade in a sample of four college students.

| **Number of Courses** | $4$ | $3$ | $5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Average Grade** | $80$ | $85$ | $75$ | $72$ |

We can collect this data in a matrix so that each column reports the number of courses and the average grade of a single student:

![](images/8a/8a489e90c10dbb65c2f5e005c32677696073cc63203116ed07d445a91d7f2d32.svg)

The matrix $X$ is called the **observation matrix.**

Suppose we want to determine the mean number of courses and the mean average grade of this sample. The **sample mean vector,** denoted $\mathbf m,$ is a vector containing these values. The sample mean vector is given by

$$
\mathbf{m} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{x}_i,
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n$ are the individual observations (columns of $X$).

From our matrix above, we have that  

![](images/45/4549af29f9356865dc9f3edb67960da00a4007a71281778d4a273a1a6eb0dbf9.svg)

Therefore, the sample mean vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{4}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 80\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 85\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 75\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 72\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 312\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the average number of courses is $4,$ and the average final grade is $78.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "652defa1-c802-5dbd-9ed9-7d863bd020a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6079 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e325102-149c-5fb3-b355-d46756b13060" :step/math-academy-id 36980 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163041}} {:db/id 17592186163041 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162094 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161907 :question/id #uuid "5f949e10-0d73-50c8-9f41-73a0d0f78e29" :question/math-academy-id "e-9833"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f930dfb2-a688-5dbe-9233-09dbcd2ba383" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048896} {:db/id 17592186050136} {:db/id 17592186050606}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162352} {:db/id 17592186162357} {:db/id 17592186512864} {:db/id 17592186512927} {:db/id 17592186512934} {:db/id 17592186512954}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Sample Mean of an Observation Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "5ccead82-f536-5ecc-ad47-7e72852fc8a0" :step/math-academy-id 36981 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163057}} {:db/id 17592186163042 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162095 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161908 :question/id #uuid "bd9fe016-cd5f-5e65-b388-35725ac0fbf4" :question/math-academy-id "e-9834"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dc84d72a-b9f3-5f99-aa23-31cfe6910d49" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049126} {:db/id 17592186050145} {:db/id 17592186050407} {:db/id 17592186050727}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162354} {:db/id 17592186162355} {:db/id 17592186410431} {:db/id 17592186512872} {:db/id 17592186512893} {:db/id 17592186512915}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Covariance Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "b20cf4dd-9e6f-553b-bdb8-e16bac07f0be" :step/math-academy-id 36982} {:db/id 17592186163043 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163311 :tutorial/content "Let's consider again the mean-deviation matrix for the students' data we found previously:

![](images/1f/1f5440b7ae08ffd19bdae816854c236afe3ca254d5bd23e26f15e34cd9c9feb2.svg)

Calculating the product $B B^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 7 & -3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -10 \\ -10 & 98\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let's analyze what we've obtained:

- The entry in the first row and first column (${\color{red}2}$) is the sum of the squares of the mean deviations of the number of courses.

- The entry in the second row and second column (${\color{blue}98}$) is the sum of the squares of the mean deviations of the final grades.

- The off-diagonal entries (${\color{purple}-10}$) are the sum of the products of the mean deviations.

Since there were $4$ observations in total, if we divide each entry by $4-1=3,$  we will get a matrix $C$ with the *sample variances* in the diagonal and the *sample covariance* in the off-diagonal positions:

![](images/7d/7d0216b462e1bf7dc34d638a7a0de30fcf063ce39d1865b45f85b526ba7bd0a8.svg)

This matrix is called the **covariance matrix** of the data.

In general, the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C = \dfrac{1}{n-1} B B^T,
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations." :tutorial/id #uuid "53d475a6-4449-56eb-8cf7-736ae440e1a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6080 :tutorial/title "The Covariance Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "f03f6d4f-4aba-584a-86ea-090a017828ca" :step/math-academy-id 36983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163042}} {:db/id 17592186163044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162096 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161909 :question/id #uuid "bdef2fdc-0a38-5bfa-9bc6-7ca50e8c10ef" :question/math-academy-id "e-9835"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e91708c9-67e2-5228-84fd-1f4ea60064ac" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162353} {:db/id 17592186162358} {:db/id 17592186512887} {:db/id 17592186512933} {:db/id 17592186512958}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Mean-Deviation Form of an Observation Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "a74161b0-4fa2-5cab-a830-1e6a769934fd" :step/math-academy-id 36984 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163043}} {:db/id 17592186163057 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163321 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we studied data that reported the number of courses selected and the average grades of a sample of four college students. The observation matrix for this data was

![](images/9b/9bdfe848443d0014461cc51e2decfbed8dc151a72edb34825dd33ac964ed6b2f.svg)

The individual observations are

![](images/3f/3f935ba5f9adea7f75a63642837a3b993286f9535d5bf1842ce3a2267413c6bc.svg)

We also found the sample mean vector 

![](images/26/261e1d746aafa95ac2f7a6d1ff36a741ff5ae37ba738f75b451a542baed1c5fc.svg)

One thing we can do with this data is to check how much each observation differs from the mean values. To do that, we compute the difference between each observation and the sample mean vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 80\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 85\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{4} & ={x}_{4}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 72\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We collect these differences in a new matrix, as follows:

![](images/83/831e698a632d40ab447c75a3b169e29c6ae8ab10c6600d838bd699a38e837931.svg)

The matrix $B$ is the **mean-deviation form** of $X.$ It's often easier to work with the mean-deviation form, especially if the original data contains large numbers.

Notice that the mean of a mean-deviation form equals the zero vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{B} & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fcfec935-52c3-571d-b471-9a1be7383ff6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6143 :tutorial/title "Mean-Deviation Form"} :step/id #uuid "8e871f51-8d02-5990-9d6d-f5e78d503fb5" :step/math-academy-id 37301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163044}}] :activity/title "The Sample Covariance Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162232} {:db/id 17592186163040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163310 :tutorial/content "The table below describes the number of classes taken per semester and the average final grade in a sample of four college students.

| **Number of Courses** | $4$ | $3$ | $5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Average Grade** | $80$ | $85$ | $75$ | $72$ |

We can collect this data in a matrix so that each column reports the number of courses and the average grade of a single student:

![](images/8a/8a489e90c10dbb65c2f5e005c32677696073cc63203116ed07d445a91d7f2d32.svg)

The matrix $X$ is called the **observation matrix.**

Suppose we want to determine the mean number of courses and the mean average grade of this sample. The **sample mean vector,** denoted $\mathbf m,$ is a vector containing these values. The sample mean vector is given by

$$
\mathbf{m} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{x}_i,
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n$ are the individual observations (columns of $X$).

From our matrix above, we have that  

![](images/45/4549af29f9356865dc9f3edb67960da00a4007a71281778d4a273a1a6eb0dbf9.svg)

Therefore, the sample mean vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{4}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 80\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 85\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 75\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 72\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 312\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the average number of courses is $4,$ and the average final grade is $78.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "652defa1-c802-5dbd-9ed9-7d863bd020a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6079 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e325102-149c-5fb3-b355-d46756b13060" :step/math-academy-id 36980 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163041}} {:db/id 17592186163310 :tutorial/content "The table below describes the number of classes taken per semester and the average final grade in a sample of four college students.

The observation matrix for this data was

![](images/9b/9bdfe848443d0014461cc51e2decfbed8dc151a72edb34825dd33ac964ed6b2f.svg)

The individual observations are

![](images/3f/3f935ba5f9adea7f75a63642837a3b993286f9535d5bf1842ce3a2267413c6bc.svg)

We also found the sample mean vector 

![](images/26/261e1d746aafa95ac2f7a6d1ff36a741ff5ae37ba738f75b451a542baed1c5fc.svg)

One thing we can do with this data is to check how much each observation differs from the mean values. To do that, we compute the difference between each observation and the sample mean vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 80\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 85\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{4} & ={x}_{4}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 72\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We collect these differences in a new matrix, as follows:

![](images/83/831e698a632d40ab447c75a3b169e29c6ae8ab10c6600d838bd699a38e837931.svg)

The matrix $B$ is the **mean-deviation form** of $X.$ It's often easier to work with the mean-deviation form, especially if the original data contains large numbers.

Notice that the mean of a mean-deviation form equals the zero vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{B} & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fcfec935-52c3-571d-b471-9a1be7383ff6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6143 :tutorial/title "Mean-Deviation Form"} :step/id #uuid "8e871f51-8d02-5990-9d6d-f5e78d503fb5" :step/math-academy-id 37301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163044}} {:db/id 17592186163042 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162095 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161908 :question/id #uuid "bd9fe016-cd5f-5e65-b388-35725ac0fbf4" :question/math-academy-id "e-9834"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dc84d72a-b9f3-5f99-aa23-31cfe6910d49" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049126} {:db/id 17592186050145} {:db/id 17592186050407} {:db/id 17592186050727}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162354} {:db/id 17592186162355} {:db/id 17592186410431} {:db/id 17592186512872} {:db/id 17592186512893} {:db/id 17592186512915}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Covariance Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "b20cf4dd-9e6f-553b-bdb8-e16bac07f0be" :step/math-academy-id 36982} {:db/id 17592186163043 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163311 :tutorial/content "Let's consider again the mean-deviation matrix for the students' data we found previously:

![](images/1f/1f5440b7ae08ffd19bdae816854c236afe3ca254d5bd23e26f15e34cd9c9feb2.svg)

Calculating the product $B B^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 7 & -3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -10 \\ -10 & 98\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let's analyze what we've obtained:

- The entry in the first row and first column (${\color{red}2}$) is the sum of the squares of the mean deviations of the number of courses.

- The entry in the second row and second column (${\color{blue}98}$) is the sum of the squares of the mean deviations of the final grades.

- The off-diagonal entries (${\color{purple}-10}$) are the sum of the products of the mean deviations.

Since there were $4$ observations in total, if we divide each entry by $4-1=3,$  we will get a matrix $C$ with the *sample variances* in the diagonal and the *sample covariance* in the off-diagonal positions:

![](images/7d/7d0216b462e1bf7dc34d638a7a0de30fcf063ce39d1865b45f85b526ba7bd0a8.svg)

This matrix is called the **covariance matrix** of the data.

In general, the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C = \dfrac{1}{n-1} B B^T,
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations." :tutorial/id #uuid "53d475a6-4449-56eb-8cf7-736ae440e1a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6080 :tutorial/title "The Covariance Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "f03f6d4f-4aba-584a-86ea-090a017828ca" :step/math-academy-id 36983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163042}} {:db/id 17592186163311 :tutorial/content "Let's consider again the mean-deviation matrix for the students' data we found previously:

{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1))-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1))(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+D) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2D \\  & =({x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$"} {:db/id 17592186375986 :question/id #uuid "a3ba8f8e-9db5-5eee-b179-738a991a847a" :question/math-academy-id "q-14743"} {:db/id 17592186392715 :question/id #uuid Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?" :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$

The rate of growth in the number of people $P(t)$ infected with the flu is jointly proportional to the number of people who have the flu at time $t,$ measured in days,  and the number of uninfected people. If the constant of proportionality is $0.6,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$" :question/worked-solution "Since the growth rate of infected people is *jointly* proportional to the number of people who have the flu at time $t,$ and the number of uninfected people, the number of infected people follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.6,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=700\,000.$ Therefore, the number of people who have the flu is given by the equation

{:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506451}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A city is tracking the number of bikes available in a bike-share station.
They observe that bikes are returned to the station at a rate $r(t)$ given by the function

$$
r(t)=5{t}^{3}+2t,
$$

where $r(t)$ is measured in bikes per hour, and $t>0$ is the time in hours since tracking began.
At the same time, $4$ bikes are rented from the station each hour.

If there were initially $100$ bikes at the station, find the expression that gives $B(t),$ the number of bikes at the station $t$ hours after tracking began.

$B(t)=\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}\,+$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The number of bikes is increasing at a rate of $r(t)$ bikes per hour and is decreasing at a rate of $4$ bikes per hour. Therefore, the **rate of change** $R(t)$ of the number of bikes is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-4 \\  & =5{t}^{3}+2t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total number $B(t)$ of bikes after $t$ hours, we apply the second fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =B(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =100+{\int }_{0}^{t}(5{x}^{3}+2x-4)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To ensure that our final function is a function of $t$ only, we use a different variable ($x$) for the integration.

We can simplify the expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =100+{\int }_{0}^{t}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{t}2x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{t}4\,\text{d}x \\  & =100+{5\,\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{t}+{2\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{t}-4x{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =100+\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}+\,{t}^{2}-4t+100\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186506580 :question/id #uuid "b1c05acb-14b2-5a23-a0fb-57fef367611e" :question/math-academy-id "q-349973" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "256" :db/id 17592186506332}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506332} :answer-field/id #uuid "bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506469}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The rate at which water flows into a tank is given by the function

$$
r(t)=6t+10,
$$

where $r(t)$ is measured in liters per hour and $t>0$ is the time in hours since $1\,\text{p.m}.$
Water is also draining from the tank at a steady rate of $8$ liters per hour.

If there were $200$ liters of water in the tank at $1\,\text{p.m},$ how many liters of water will be there at $5\,\text{p.m}?$

There will be 
{{field-1}}  liters of water in the tank at $5\,\text{p.m}.$" :question/worked-solution "Water is flowing into the tank at a rate of $6t+10$ liters per hour and is draining at a rate of $8$ liters per hour. Therefore, the **rate of change** in the amount of water (call it $R(t)$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-8 \\  & =6t+10-8 \\  & =6t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the **total amount of water** after $t$ hours (call it $T(t)$), we apply the second fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =200+{\int }_{0}^{t}(6x+2)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To ensure that $T$ is a function of $t$ only, we use a different variable ($x$) for the integration. 

To find out the amount of water after $4$ hours ($5\,\text{p.m}$), we substitute $t=4$ into the above and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(4) & =200+{\int }_{0}^{4}(6x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =200+(3{x}^{2}+2x){|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =200+[(3\cdot 16+8)-0] \\  & =200+56 \\  & =256\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there will be $256$ liters of water in the tank at $5\,\text{p.m}.$"} {:db/id 17592186147399 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147335 :question/id #uuid 17592186101725 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102033 :tutorial/content "A differential equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt} = ky(a-y),
$$

where $y=y(t)$ is called a **logistic growth equation.** 

Note the following:

- $a$ is a positive constant called the **carrying capacity**.

- $k$ is a positive constant of proportionality.

A typical solution curve $y = y(t)$ to this equation is shown below:

![](images/0f/0f416479bbf72d3b9c1bf48861883e0e77bbc1c1d60d7fa48fb89e6f21c104eb.png)

We will learn more about the structure of the solution curves in future lessons. But for now, it's helpful to realize that for all $t,$ we have

$$
0 < y(t) < a.
$$

 

An example of a logistic growth equation is

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt} = 10y(50-y).
$$

Here, $k = 10$ and the carrying capacity is $a=50.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f5791475-4f91-5859-9d5b-1f20283522ea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 982 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186101800}} {:db/id 17592186101800 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101996 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to create a model of the deer population in a forest. Let's denote the number of deer in the forest at time $t$ as $P(t).$

Imagine that we have two factors that influence the size of the deer population:

- Unconstrained, the rate at which the deer population increases is proportional to the size of the deer population (i.e., exponential growth).

- However, as the deer population increases, food resources become more scarce. The forest cannot sustain an arbitrarily large number of deer. Therefore, we must specify the maximum number of deer that the forest can sustain. This maximum number is the forest's carrying capacity, denoted $a,$ as before.

Therefore, we say that the rate of change of the deer population $P(t)$ is **jointly proportional** to *both* the deer population $P$ itself *and* the remaining room for growth, which is $a-P.$ This gives us the logistic growth equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d P}{\textrm d t} = kP(a-P).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "136097ca-5c5c-587e-918d-decbcb156cbf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5720 :tutorial/title "Modeling Situations Using a Logistic Growth Equation"} :step/id #uuid "80e2d4b5-6d7a-5649-8978-26fea11f0ae7" :step/math-academy-id 35117 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101785}}] :activity/title "Logistic Growth Models With First-Order ODEs" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186101030} {:db/id 17592186101725 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102033 :tutorial/content "A differential equation of the form

Let's denote the number of deer in the forest at time $t$ as $P(t).$

Imagine that we have two factors that influence the size of the deer population:

- Unconstrained, the rate at which the deer population increases is proportional to the size of the deer population (i.e., exponential growth).

- However, as the deer population increases, food resources become more scarce. The forest cannot sustain an arbitrarily large number of deer. Therefore, we must specify the maximum number of deer that the forest can sustain. This maximum number is the forest's carrying capacity, denoted $a,$ as before.

Therefore, we say that the rate of change of the deer population $P(t)$ is **jointly proportional** to *both* the deer population $P$ itself *and* the remaining room for growth, which is $a-P.$ This gives us the logistic growth equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d P}{\textrm d t} = kP(a-P).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "136097ca-5c5c-587e-918d-decbcb156cbf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5720 :tutorial/title "Modeling Situations Using a Logistic Growth Equation"} :step/id #uuid "80e2d4b5-6d7a-5649-8978-26fea11f0ae7" :step/math-academy-id 35117 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101785}} {:db/id 17592186101996 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to create a model of the deer population in a forest. A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.6,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=700\,000.$ Therefore, the number of people who have the flu is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.6P(700\,000-P).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "876b041e-48ee-59ed-9570-27aae1e87501" :step/next {:db/id 17592186524097}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d85e959-a5d2-57fb-865e-ce7038ba9c8c" :answer/type {:db/id "d7927711-e084-5b0c-97d6-05acd9686522" :topic/math-academy-id 416} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070031 :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int x^2e^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?

Let's  try. We define $u$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for integration by parts leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral  $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =x(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})+{C}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1$ is a constant of integration.
So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{8}\,x{e}^{4x}+\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}-\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}(8{x}^{2}-4x+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -\dfrac{C_1}{2}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35a2eb7b-569b-5939-bcc0-2261596617e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 901 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068951} {:db/id 17592186069905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070031 :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int x^2e^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?

Let's  try. We define $u$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for integration by parts leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral  $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =x(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})+{C}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1$ is a constant of integration.
So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{8}\,x{e}^{4x}+\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}-\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}(8{x}^{2}-4x+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -\dfrac{C_1}{2}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35a2eb7b-569b-5939-bcc0-2261596617e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 901 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "944ebf60-fe41-58ac-91a8-63c93b565add" :step/math-academy-id 655420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069906}} {:db/id 17592186070031 :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int x^2e^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?

:step/content {:db/id 17592186176988 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis. We can also obtain surfaces of revolution by rotating a curve $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.

Consider the arc of the curve $x=f(y)$ that lies between the horizontal lines $y=y_1$ and $y=y_2.$ By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis, we get a surface of revolution, as shown below on the right. How can we calculate its surface area?

![](images/e6/e61f97b06c3228bb2671429d6562e97d6cdefefb7ac1acca31867eeb440a75ff.png)

First, we divide the interval $[y_1,y_2]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{y}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $y$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](images/25/253837a6c151a74318b2e172e6db068a50d23c9cb93124588ae20a9379d9aa63.png)

If $\Delta{y}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $x=f(y).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=x=f(y).$ 

![](images/9f/9f10812beff0283e6029145b854a2faaa9b7a566751bd17514bc6817ef664dfc.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi x \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s
$$

Recall that for a curve $x = f(y),$ we can express the arc length element $\textrm d s$ as

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we can find the total surface area using the formula

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f1dd2211-511b-5b65-9250-ee6b84f0d566" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5319 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "76d50374-b9a8-5d13-90fe-031de2946fbe" :step/math-academy-id given a curve of the form $y=f(x)$ that lies between the vertical lines $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2.$ How do we calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?

Earlier, we showed that the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

For a curve $y = f(x),$ the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.

First, we divide the interval $[y_1,y_2]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{y}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $y$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](images/25/253837a6c151a74318b2e172e6db068a50d23c9cb93124588ae20a9379d9aa63.png)

If $\Delta{y}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $x=f(y).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=x=f(y).$ 

![](images/9f/9f10812beff0283e6029145b854a2faaa9b7a566751bd17514bc6817ef664dfc.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi x \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s
$$

Recall that for a curve $x = f(y),$ we can express the arc length element $\textrm d s$ as

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we can find the total surface area using the formula

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f1dd2211-511b-5b65-9250-ee6b84f0d566" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5319 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186176718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186175978 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175828 :question/id #uuid "6ee942e8-9fb9-5dfb-8f9c-aea1dd6d53ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-8907"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bff48a7c-66d6-55e8-99a1-ae8c80925335" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049272} {:db/id 17592186050393}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176207} {:db/id 17592186176233} {:db/id 17592186244252} {:db/id 17592186244255} {:db/id 17592186262634} {:db/id 17592186362668} {:db/id 17592186387692} {:db/id 17592186434224} {:db/id 17592186434226}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y"} :step/id #uuid "b8f345d7-4e41-5e19-b9f6-352cfd48cc6a" :step/math-academy-id 33268 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176763}} {:db/id 17592186176763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177009 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given a curve of the form $y=f(x)$ that lies between the vertical lines $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2.$ How do we calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?

$$
r(t) = 600e^{-3t},
$$

where $r(t)$ is measured in liters per hour, and $t > 0$ is the time (in hours) since the water flow started. 

Suppose we want to know how much water enters the tank between $1$ and $2$ hours. 

Let's take note of the following:

- We're interested in the amount of water that enters the tank between $t=1$ and $t=2.$ In other words, we want the **net change in volume** between these times. We're *not* finding the total volume of water in the tank.

- We're given the **rate of change of volume** $r(t).$

To find the net change in volume, we integrate $r(t)$ between the two limits. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}600{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & ={-\frac{600}{3}{e}^{-3t}|}_{1}^{2} \\  & ={-200{e}^{-3t}|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =-200({e}^{-6}-{e}^{-3}) \\  & =200({e}^{-3}-{e}^{-6}) \\  & =200{e}^{-6}({e}^{3}-1)\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60a3bf2a-7142-575f-8381-dfb70827c7c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2744 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "62e34955-26a4-56d7-b473-2f2540475511" :step/math-academy-id 13518 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148236}} {:db/id 17592186148236 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147397 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147333 :question/id #uuid "a3030491-423d-5633-8208-b373bfee3b06" :question/math-academy-id "e-3892"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b19641aa-8e39-5348-8565-9f4ce030d18f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050200}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186148011} {:db/id 17592186148014} {:db/id 17592186319353} {:db/id 17592186319354} {:db/id 17592186319355} {:db/id 17592186357465} {:db/id 17592186478386} {:db/id 17592186478411} {:db/id 17592186478416} {:db/id 17592186478434} {:db/id 17592186478466}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Net Change of a Function Given Its Rate of Change"} :step/id #uuid "98d275b2-d6f2-53c5-b4d7-cae25b562f1a" :step/math-academy-id 13519 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148237}} {:db/id 17592186148237 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148739 :tutorial/content "If we're interested to find the **total number** or **total amount** of some quantity, we should use the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Let's go back to the earlier example with the shopping mall (Example 1). Suppose that there are $2\,000$ people inside the mall at the moment that it opened. How many people in total are inside the mall after $2$ hours?

We already know that the **rate of change** in the number of people is $R(t).$ Therefore, the **total number of people** in the mall at time $t$, which we'll call $T(t)$ is given by:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}r(x)-25\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

**Important**: You'll notice that we changed the variable of integration from $t$ to $x.$ This is to ensure that $T$ comes out as a function of $t,$ and also so we don't get confused. When we have a definite integral, it does not matter which variable we use!

To work out how many people are inside the mall at $t=2,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2) & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{2}r(x)-25\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\,000+{{{\int }_{0}^{2}r(x)-25\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{850} \\  & =2\,000+850 \\  & =2\,850\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02950c6c-bf43-5c34-885c-8da2caa06fbf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2745 :tutorial/title "Finding Total Amounts Given Rates of Change"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "To calculate the arc length of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ between the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2,$ we can use the formula

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

For example, suppose that we want to find the arc length of the polar curve $r = 2,$ where $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$ The required arc length is shown in blue in the picture below.

![](images/e9/e91cd717469db56426e39e8975aa04710ff2357c7a0d5de9d20f99bc5edcbb1c.png)

We will use the formula to compute the arc length. Since $r=2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 0,
$$

and therefore, the arc length can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3}2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3} \\  & =2(\frac{2\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "46d71df2-8000-5586-bb24-748b23a02ce3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1141 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cc4e82f8-a2bd-59bb-ab26-acf1b38e6eba" :step/math-academy-id :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula to compute the arc length bounded by a polar curve:

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{ r^2 + \left( \frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} \right)^2} \:\textrm{d}\theta
$$

But where does this formula come from? Let's start with the familiar formula for the arc length of a parametric curve:

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}t
$$

A polar curve is really just a parametric curve with parameter $\theta$ and parametric equations given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the arc length formula for a parametric function with parameter $\theta,$ we have

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}\theta .
$$

Since $x = r \cos \theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since $y=r\sin \theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $L,$ we reach the desired formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1821e80d-8c1b-5d2f-88dd-c207d2c3d99f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1144 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Main Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a2419f97-10bb-5949-b766-7c403f31ea78" :step/math-academy-id 617636}] :activity/title "The Arc Length of a Polar Curve" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092470} {:db/id 17592186093309 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093361 :tutorial/content "To calculate the arc length of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ between the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2,$ we can use the formula

17592186093312}} {:db/id 17592186093312 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093364 :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula to compute the arc length bounded by a polar curve:

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{ r^2 + \left( \frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} \right)^2} \:\textrm{d}\theta
$$

But where does this formula come from? Let's start with the familiar formula for the arc length of a parametric curve:

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}t
$$

A polar curve is really just a parametric curve with parameter $\theta$ and parametric equations given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the arc length formula for a parametric function with parameter $\theta,$ we have

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}\theta .
$$

Since $x = r \cos \theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since $y=r\sin \theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $L,$ we reach the desired formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1821e80d-8c1b-5d2f-88dd-c207d2c3d99f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1144 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Main Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a2419f97-10bb-5949-b766-7c403f31ea78" :step/math-academy-id 617636} {:db/id 17592186093364 :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula to compute the arc length bounded by a polar curve:

:question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e4403343-b5c6-5fde-abd9-266da3d46e06" :step/next {:db/id 17592186531669}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ebc83588-25b8-5ff4-bfc0-bce39c4a0f4f" :answer/type {:db/id
