$\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y={e}^{-t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0cdae9f2-99ba-523d-86fd-08256e29cd00" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515645}} {:db/id 17592186515643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20f3235b-60e2-5c23-a6d1-2912bfc76c91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186358041} {:answer/id #uuid "b7fdac84-5c94-5bcb-847f-c1a99a8c5411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359347} {:answer/id #uuid "bde855a4-7fc2-52c3-af6f-b2e1fd0d6c05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359405} {:answer/id #uuid "dc8b8503-66f4-52dd-b74c-bee16b502323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359689} {:answer/id #uuid "e953648a-9a4f-5892-9fbd-2c82540d2fdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359825}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359405} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b3efa02-f1ae-5df0-98fd-0df55d2c7698" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360170}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9d03333b-22a3-579a-b479-87085056a6c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95059" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "386e3776-9252-5f0e-9289-19a65b4311b4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515689}} {:db/id 17592186515645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186445680 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445652} {:answer/id #uuid "76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445657} {:answer/id #uuid "869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445658} {:answer/id #uuid "9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(2\pi )" :db/id 17592186445662} {:answer/id #uuid "e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445670}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445652} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186445676}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/math-academy-id "q-36234" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3a4200b6-903e-5981-924d-9535282a3f9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515643}} {:db/id 17592186515689 :step/content {:db/id 17592186515530 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0618c56b-92f8-5743-9e32-328933507a90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}+{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186514887} {:answer/id #uuid "42831ed2-f44c-506e-a16d-0e06ead786c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2t}-{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186515014} {:answer/id #uuid "581a6ccb-d929-5a4c-abd5-314717c764d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2t}+t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186515068} {:answer/id #uuid "b182ff13-9dbc-5c38-8d5b-05e109460201" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{t}+t}}" :db/id 17592186515243} {:answer/id #uuid "b6bd0e4e-b413-5783-9897-cec63d3177bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{{e}^{t}+t}}" :db/id 17592186515258}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186515068} :answer-field/id #uuid "9eb54adf-64fe-5825-9ef0-62336c5f858a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186515471}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2becf284-e142-5ae3-80f6-d208696ea202" :question/math-academy-id "q-95068" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\,j \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t}+t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bf608e7a-0173-58ee-a61e-d120aeb92841" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515711}} {:db/id 17592186515711 :step/content {:db/id 17592186485588 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "131e1312-3232-541a-a772-9a4195876e08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484854} {:answer/id #uuid "1cf61e8f-1cbe-5cf7-b7de-cb285c2945df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484868} {:answer/id #uuid "54a8785f-b684-5fbf-ab5e-7a2651308e2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485006} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1155ed-ffcf-5482-9835-4e132b93d976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485086} {:answer/id #uuid "7d4e5d76-01d4-5027-9d0b-5f4455a3c94c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485006} :answer-field/id #uuid "26f9db34-f1fa-54a6-9839-7f297b6a756c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186485384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eabe5e6a-dc85-5118-84d2-9aa9f31a6a23" :question/math-academy-id "q-95086" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i+2t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=2t$ and $z={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$

$$

"q-36234" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3a4200b6-903e-5981-924d-9535282a3f9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515643}} {:db/id 17592186515643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20f3235b-60e2-5c23-a6d1-2912bfc76c91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186358041} {:answer/id #uuid "b7fdac84-5c94-5bcb-847f-c1a99a8c5411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359347} {:answer/id #uuid "bde855a4-7fc2-52c3-af6f-b2e1fd0d6c05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359405} {:answer/id #uuid "dc8b8503-66f4-52dd-b74c-bee16b502323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359689} {:answer/id #uuid "e953648a-9a4f-5892-9fbd-2c82540d2fdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359825}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359405} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b3efa02-f1ae-5df0-98fd-0df55d2c7698" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360170}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9d03333b-22a3-579a-b479-87085056a6c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95059" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=2t$ and $z={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2t(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)(1+t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fee8b366-8b24-5d5f-8a6e-56a6d4fdb53d"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8113f0c1-13bf-5ab2-9884-6d72597b1b88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident "![](images/36/36b985c811eb28d8220017c6b7407b3a104554d785dafdb35f17553c262bdc35.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134086 :question/id #uuid "e1880828-25c5-5042-afdb-e835de5c511c" :question/math-academy-id "q-124283" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133892 :knowledge-point/id #uuid Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(4,0)$ to the point $(-4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186527925 :question/id #uuid "2f9d1bf2-2ca6-5610-aed1-5f5054aae288" :question/math-academy-id "q-124272"} {:db/id 17592186133893 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,0)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(0+t(1-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & =1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134084 :question/id #uuid "cb08f302-8cb5-5978-acbb-0bba1cddced3" :question/math-academy-id "q-124123"} {:db/id 17592186259602 :question/id #uuid Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(\sqrt{x-1}+y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,2)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t \\  & =\sqrt{t}-t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0) \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259606 :question/id #uuid "0f008788-4322-589f-b4f5-5bd6b468b9b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-124177"} {:db/id 17592186259619 :question/id #uuid "cdf631e5-2841-5a67-a8ff-d0eebc8b7e83" :question/math-academy-id "q-124212"} {:db/id 17592186259622 :question/id #uuid "1879edf5-1344-5830-a3f2-7e9af982bae4" :question/math-academy-id "q-124217"} {:db/id 17592186259646 :question/id #uuid "11aa222d-e9ea-5ecd-ab97-032f5281bcab" :question/math-academy-id "q-124273"} {:db/id 17592186369272 :question/id #uuid "bb41f199-2f33-5f68-9a53-dffe3c93ab84" :question/math-academy-id "q-124268"} {:db/id 17592186411859 :question/id #uuid "58242fe6-4f94-5872-a2af-27a25e52256a" :question/math-academy-id "q-124278"} {:db/id 17592186527980 :question/id #uuid "ada3d128-ac86-51c2-88c8-3e672e4cad88" :question/math-academy-id "q-124172"} {:db/id 17592186050666} {:db/id 17592186050687 :topic/difficulty 0.7115353819465683 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429196 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral. 

Suppose that $C$ is a path in the $xy$-plane with initial point $A$ and terminal point $B.$ The line integral of the function $f(x,y)$ **with respect to $\boldsymbol x$** along the path $C$ is denoted

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.
$$

To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing $C$ from $A$ to $B.$ At each point $P$ that lies on $C,$ we project the point on $f$ that lies directly above $P$ onto the plane $y=0.$ Doing this for every point on $C$ traces out a curve. The line integral of $f$ with respect to $x$ gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the $x$-axis.

![](images/62/62c07a36cbf79459021ee7be125536a8f9c1bc3c193a99eabfcd3fc851b8eb0c.png)

To calculate a line integral with respect to $x,$ we must first parameterize $C$ using a parameter $t\in [a,b].$ Then, we apply the change of variables formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f1254b7-43b2-5b19-b5e9-cf33ff6cffe8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5812 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1087} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097624 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097800 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the sequence $a_n,$ given by

$$
a_n = \dfrac {n^3 + 5 n}{2 n^3 - n^2}, \qquad\ n\geq 1,
$$

and suppose that we want to determine the **limit of the sequence** $a_n.$ In the context of sequences, this means to work out $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n.$

Finding the limit of a rational sequence $a_n$ is very similar to finding the horizontal asymptotes of a rational function. We divide the numerator and the denominator by the variable part of the dominant term in the denominator. 

In our case, the variable part of the dominant term in the denominator is $n^3,$ so we divide the numerator and denominator by $n^3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{3}+5n}{2{n}^{3}-{n}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}}+\frac{5n}{{n}^{3}})}{(\frac{2{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}}-\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(1+\frac{5}{{n}^{2}})}{(2-\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{1+0}{2-0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the finite limit exists, we say that the sequence **converges** and its limit is $\dfrac 1 2.$

If the limit of a sequence does *not* exist, then we say that the sequence **diverges**." :tutorial/id #uuid "67373759-4b5b-5913-9a45-f853199756d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1145 :tutorial/title :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The solution to the inequality $-9a\le -54$ is $a${{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The variable $a$ is being *multiplied* by $-9.$ To isolate $a,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-9.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9a\,\, & \le \,\,-54 \\ \frac{-9a}{-9}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-54}{-9} \\ \frac{-9a}{-9}\,\, & \ge \,\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-9$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-9a}{-9} & \ge 6 \\ \frac{\cancel{-9}a}{\cancel{-9}} & \ge 6 \\ a & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a\ge 6.$"} {:db/id 17592186507412 :question/id #uuid "2d8f9e5d-ffea-59b8-9f7c-2f9037766a19" :question/math-academy-id "q-6277" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e3dff68-6795-523f-999b-07af4af3ec70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y<6" :db/id 17592186506706} {:answer/id #uuid "7668d459-4f42-5919-bb7f-fa7eec09053a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y>9" :db/id 17592186506946} {:answer/id #uuid "9074c12a-1d5b-5242-a19c-1b503006d445" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y<9" :db/id 17592186506999} {:answer/id #uuid "acb62ac6-c48e-569b-a36c-c8b94883aa98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y>-9" :db/id 17592186507060} {:answer/id #uuid "e10be7fe-3362-55cd-9dae-30e59a1d1e04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y<-9" :db/id 17592186507168}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507168} :answer-field/id #uuid "1301f956-a5f9-5af2-b9fc-78b855c39882" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507253}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-2y>18.$" :question/worked-solution "The variable $y$ is being *multiplied* by $-2.$ To isolate $y,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-2.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\,\, & <\,\,-\frac{z}{6} \\ (-6)\cdot 4\,\, & >\,\,(-6)\cdot (-\frac{z}{6}) \\ -24\,\, & >\,\,(-6)\cdot (-\frac{z}{6})\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-24\,\, & >(-6)\cdot (-\frac{z}{6}) \\ -24 & >(\cancel{-}6)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{z}{6}) \\ -24 & >6\cdot \frac{z}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $6$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}-24 & >6\cdot \frac{z}{6} \\ -24 & >\frac{6z}{6} \\ -24 & >\frac{\cancel{6}z}{\cancel{6}} \\ -24 & >z\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the inequality with the variable on the left-hand side:

$$
z<-24
$$

$$
x + 4 < 7
$$

To **solve** this inequality, we need to isolate the variable $x$ on one side.

Inequalities are just like equations because they can be solved using the addition and multiplication principles.

So, to solve this inequality, we subtract $4$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & <7 \\ x+4-4 & <7-4 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution is $x < 3.$ This tells us that any value of $x$ smaller than $3$ satisfies the original inequality.

17592186056022 :tutorial/content "We'll now learn why we must flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number. 

To help us, let's consider the following inequality:

$$
6 > 0
$$

For example:

- Multiplying the inequality by $2$ gives $12 > 0,$ which is *true*.$\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- Dividing the inequality by $2$ gives $3 > 0,$ which is also *true*. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

However, if we multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, *without* flipping the inequality sign, we get a false statement.

For example:

- Multiplying the inequality by $-2$ *without flipping the inequality sign* gives $-12 > 0,$ which is *false*. $\quad{\color{red}{\times}}$

- Dividing the inequality by $-2$ *without flipping the inequality sign* gives $-3 > 0,$ which is also *false*. $\quad{\color{red}{\times}}$

So, whenever we multiply or divide by a negative number, we need to flip the sign of the inequality for it to remain true.

- Multiplying the inequality by $-2$ *and flipping the inequality sign* gives $-12 < 0,$ which is *true*. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- Dividing the inequality by $-2$ *and flipping the sign* gives $-3 < 0,$ which is also *true*. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f9eacf1c-4f75-5dfe-a8e7-798404a6280d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8101 :tutorial/title "Why We Flip the Inequality Sign"} :step/id #uuid "e300a5cf-0bdb-5c23-9a03-3bb60a12a788" :step/math-academy-id 52070}] :activity/title "Solving One-Step Linear Inequalities" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054900} {:db/id 17592186055780 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056020 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following inequality:

$$

$$

To **solve** this inequality, we need to isolate the variable $x$ on one side.

Inequalities are just like equations because they can be solved using the addition and multiplication principles.

So, to solve this inequality, we subtract $4$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & <7 \\ x+4-4 & <7-4 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution is $x < 3.$ This tells us that any value of $x$ smaller than $3$ satisfies the original inequality.

Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9a\,\, & \le \,\,-54 \\ \frac{-9a}{-9}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-54}{-9} \\ \frac{-9a}{-9}\,\, & \ge \,\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-9$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$

$$

$$

vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281492 :question/id #uuid "4adb65fe-96f0-5d44-a083-7671cd65bedb" :question/math-academy-id "q-162540"} {:db/id 17592186281494 :question/id #uuid $$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186444619 :question/id #uuid "627a222e-9363-5b8b-b1ec-0730c89cfcbe" :question/math-academy-id "q-161193" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e7ca8ec-891f-5ccc-985b-4e4a85531ac2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186444602} {:answer/id #uuid "3ccaaf5e-0e10-5c99-a0bc-d8a834cb86f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444604} {:answer/id #uuid "a5039a5b-f9d4-5a06-b32c-4be440d0e059" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186444609} {:answer/id #uuid "c73e0516-826a-57fd-99ad-0e6ddc957f95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186444611} {:answer/id #uuid "f817a54c-d2b8-5a8f-9b28-dbefeb579916" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444615}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444611} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c6a2aa9-7d14-5b93-966f-5ef76762e118" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444616}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 3178} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167782 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168144 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle xz + y,\: x^2,\: 2y-z^2 \right\rangle\!, 
\qquad 
\mathbf{n}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left\langle 2,\: 0,\: -1 \right\rangle\!.
$$

Let's construct a surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}.$

First, we recall that if $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}((xz+y)\cdot 2+{x}^{2}\cdot 0+(2y-{z}^{2})\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2xz+2y-2y+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf n$ can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{∬}_{S}2xz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S\end{aligned}
$$

We can then evaluate this integral using the usual methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "c936101d-fbb9-594d-888c-2327d0908e71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7632 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. But first, we need a brief discussion on surface orientations." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a17f47e-f50d-578f-a41c-9e537ded3620" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7725 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "507e9c0b-b2be-5bf9-a53c-e763d7e4315b" :step/math-academy-id 657075 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167787}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186167787 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "81d0dc6b-4e76-5f80-934b-e300c50b0201" :step/math-academy-id 657086 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167788}}] :activity/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166981} {:db/id 17592186167785 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168145 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$

$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. $$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle xz + y,\: x^2,\: 2y-z^2 \right\rangle\!,

\mathbf{n}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left\langle 2,\: 0,\: -1 \right\rangle\!.
$$

Let's construct a surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}.$

First, we recall that if $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}((xz+y)\cdot 2+{x}^{2}\cdot 0+(2y-{z}^{2})\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2xz+2y-2y+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf n$ can be written as follows:

$$

$$

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "15c5dca7-7c90-57e5-be91-60bf5e44e76b" :step/math-academy-id 657076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167786}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} {:db/id 17592186167788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166487 :question/id #uuid "35c3c9ba-60b0-5bcf-8e9c-2862ece44e7e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12454"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9a62365-4278-557f-ba76-caa31abe7869" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167129} {:db/id 17592186167130} {:db/id 17592186167131} {:db/id 17592186278417} {:db/id 17592186278418} {:db/id 17592186281387} {:db/id 17592186281388} {:db/id 17592186281492} {:db/id 17592186281494} {:db/id 17592186281496} {:db/id 17592186369894} {:db/id 17592186369908} {:db/id 17592186421235} {:db/id 17592186421237} {:db/id 17592186421241} {:db/id 17592186444618} {:db/id 17592186444619}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "99f84857-19d8-532f-b1f8-974d1ed142df" :step/math-academy-id 657087} {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3a45ce20-02a0-56e8-9b38-add2ba9480d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7733 :tutorial/title "The Fundamental Vector Product for a Horizontal Plane"} {:db/id 17592186362413 :tutorial/content "If we wish to find the flux through a tilted plane, we should first calculate the unit normal vector to this plane.

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186444620} :activity/id #uuid "0bdff687-f8d4-5855-9373-b5ab9e4534b8" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050188 :topic/id #uuid "34eb87b9-7036-55c0-88eb-1b1efbd11584" :topic/math-academy-id 3178} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186444620 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167127 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "51f5f2fd-94a6-51c3-ac48-99d59a93e907" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y+z" :db/id 17592186444605} {:answer/id #uuid "8524a039-125d-5c28-8aaa-2b417ce25d91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y+z" :db/id 17592186444606} {:answer/id #uuid "a0cc803d-28d2-5c8a-ad4d-e88ee6c149ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-y-z" :db/id 17592186444608} {:answer/id #uuid "ad810e29-dc47-543e-aeb1-8297ce882407" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z-x" :db/id 17592186444610} {:answer/id #uuid "e9761621-383d-53ec-8615-e110f65c1ad5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y+2z" :db/id 17592186444613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444610} :answer-field/id #uuid "63f86b8b-b32a-5de1-8bfa-b93d1b01899d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186163840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "44a48f57-f74b-5294-bb24-4cee5d89d1d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-161149" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,.

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(2z-(x+y)+(y-z)) \\  & =\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}z-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "03b4b191-1c32-5328-8c44-46701817acdf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444623}} {:db/id 17592186444621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186444618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23676b92-59ce-549e-bb44-0ce2c22aff60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186444601} {:answer/id #uuid "30a14e60-74d3-59a0-9d7c-8bfb0dc4a3c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444603} {:answer/id #uuid "8c7915a4-09c6-54d8-8b86-d3abcf6997b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444607} {:answer/id #uuid "ca06b212-b30b-58a7-bceb-f7e5db8c00f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444612} {:answer/id #uuid "f6e593f7-c2c1-5fc5-8a3d-c699694f0c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444614} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ac4cbf3-d6da-5e60-8eb4-cf067330135d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444617}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2ae7b222-1017-5e06-9f85-8323117b3184" :question/math-academy-id "q-162158" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+2y+1$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0ad1dc8f-1c73-5500-a47a-c0fda9ab766e"} {:db/id 17592186444622 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2720bb2d-ef3c-5bd3-b5d1-47e2a36e5b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy+yz+xz" :db/id 17592186275834} {:answer/id #uuid "30f13b93-277e-5c15-b9c8-932581f5f992" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-2yz+xz" :db/id 17592186275912} {:answer/id #uuid "3b883b06-8332-53dc-bb7f-68fb90e59ae4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3xz-yz" :db/id 17592186275997} {:answer/id #uuid "74a4ce69-d793-5db1-9424-5b3b421ad0a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186276532} {:answer/id #uuid "8f857f74-c7bf-534b-90d2-dc5735bc9d12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-yz+2xz" :db/id 17592186276777}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276777} :answer-field/id #uuid "74b1826a-ee9f-5272-9977-4058c1ea92ea" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277932}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fe4ccf73-c8f1-5e87-8e15-f27def60e911" :question/math-academy-id "q-161200" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "627a222e-9363-5b8b-b1ec-0730c89cfcbe" :question/math-academy-id "q-161193" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b60e2d93-3137-5009-9f82-8e66614f6b08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444624}} {:db/id 17592186444621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186444618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23676b92-59ce-549e-bb44-0ce2c22aff60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186444601} {:answer/id #uuid "30a14e60-74d3-59a0-9d7c-8bfb0dc4a3c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444603} {:answer/id #uuid "8c7915a4-09c6-54d8-8b86-d3abcf6997b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444607} {:answer/id #uuid "ca06b212-b30b-58a7-bceb-f7e5db8c00f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444612} {:answer/id #uuid "f6e593f7-c2c1-5fc5-8a3d-c699694f0c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444614} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ac4cbf3-d6da-5e60-8eb4-cf067330135d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444617}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2ae7b222-1017-5e06-9f85-8323117b3184" :question/math-academy-id "q-162158" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+2y+1$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0ad1dc8f-1c73-5500-a47a-c0fda9ab766e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23676b92-59ce-549e-bb44-0ce2c22aff60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" $$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩\,.

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2{z}^{2}-x+2(y-{z}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{2y-x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2y-x}{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{S}2y-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}

"cf643e99-f61d-5e66-8afd-c5e23c2c54df" :step/math-academy-id 26196 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172869}} {:db/id 17592186172979 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173195 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the differential equation $y' = -4xy.$ The slope field for this equation is shown below.

![](images/a4/a47ec9497553fdcc9d20607f309bdaee00bb1fc0af4d39dea8a6a843a2e417e6.png)

Let's see how much information we can gather about the differential equation by referring *only* to its slope field.

- First, note that the slope field has neither vertical nor horizontal symmetry. Therefore, the associated differential equation must be of the form $y' = f(x,y).$ Indeed, the equation $y' =-4xy$ is of this form.

- Second, notice that the solution curves appear to have stationary points along the lines $x=0$ and $y=0.$ This means that the right-hand side of our differential equation must evaluate to zero on these lines. Indeed, this is true of our equation.

![](images/7b/7beccfd6840c2715bfd3c923f4fe6ac05bdf07f9ed65931b016efd937b1a0b63.png)

- Third, the lines $x=0$ and $y=0$ split the plane into four regions. The slopes of the solution curves in each of these regions are summarized in the table below.

| $y > 0$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y <       0$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ |
|  | $x<       0$ | $x> 0$ |

Notice that the sign of $f(x,y)$ in the four regions agrees with the above table:

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is positive in the second and fourth quadrants, and

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is negative in the first and third quadrants." :tutorial/id #uuid "dd16b3e1-53b3-55bf-af84-540daaefde15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9018b840-14fc-5403-a85b-0696a121416b" :step/math-academy-id 34802 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172982}} {:db/id 17592186172982 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172082 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171888 :question/id #uuid "95746e3f-5cdf-58e2-8dbb-39b3cbe5cfc1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9356"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cd82d96b-34d5-5d20-b810-7ea88b0b5797" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048489} {:db/id 17592186049722} {:db/id 17592186050480}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172566} {:db/id 17592186172568} {:db/id 17592186253664} {:db/id 17592186332800} {:db/id 17592186332801} {:db/id 17592186332803}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using Stationary Points"} :step/id #uuid "de33aa28-2c66-5a35-b972-8287ff822b59" :step/math-academy-id 35034 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172870}}] :activity/title "Analyzing Slope Fields for Nonautonomous Differential Equations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172172} {:db/id 17592186172979 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173195 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the differential equation $y' = -4xy.$ The slope field for this equation is shown below.

:tutorial/content "Let's consider the differential equation $y' = -4xy.$ The slope field for this equation is shown below.

![](images/a4/a47ec9497553fdcc9d20607f309bdaee00bb1fc0af4d39dea8a6a843a2e417e6.png)

Let's see how much information we can gather about the differential equation by referring *only* to its slope field.

- First, note that the slope field has neither vertical nor horizontal symmetry. Therefore, the associated differential equation must be of the form $y' = f(x,y).$ Indeed, the equation $y' =-4xy$ is of this form.

- Second, notice that the solution curves appear to have stationary points along the lines $x=0$ and $y=0.$ This means that the right-hand side of our differential equation must evaluate to zero on these lines. Indeed, this is true of our equation.

![](images/7b/7beccfd6840c2715bfd3c923f4fe6ac05bdf07f9ed65931b016efd937b1a0b63.png)

- Third, the lines $x=0$ and $y=0$ split the plane into four regions. The slopes of the solution curves in each of these regions are summarized in the table below.

| $y > 0$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y <       0$ | $\searrow$

$({\color{red}{-}})$ | $\nearrow$

$({\color{blue}{+}})$ |
|  | $x<       0$ | $x> 0$ |

Notice that the sign of $f(x,y)$ in the four regions agrees with the above table:

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is positive in the second and fourth quadrants, and

- $f(x,y)=-4xy$ is negative in the first and third quadrants." :tutorial/id #uuid "dd16b3e1-53b3-55bf-af84-540daaefde15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id
